title: Time gained
hookLine: how much time you gain by not watching what your neighbor says or does (Meditations 4.18)
carry: run straight along the line, without swerving

cards: A woman stands at her kitchen window, coffee going cold. Across the street, the neighbors have a new car.
She notices the color, guesses the price, wonders how they afford it, remembers what her sister said about them, then checks the clock. Twenty minutes, gone, on a life that isn't hers.
Marcus Aurelius knew the habit long before anyone carried a window onto other lives in their pocket. And he did the accounting. Today: time gained.

teach.b: How much leisure he gains, Marcus writes in the eighteenth entry of book four, who doesn't look to see what his neighbor says or does or thinks, but only at what he himself is doing, so that it may be just and holy.
The Greek word is euscholia, good leisure: time that's free. Watching others spends it. Marcus isn't saying ignore people or stop caring.
He's saying stop monitoring: checking what others are up to so you can compare, judge, or feel better or worse. It costs time, and buys almost nothing you can use.
The attention you take back goes to one question: is what I'm doing just? A carpenter looking at the next bench all day doesn't build a better chair. Then an image from the racetrack.
Don't look around at the dark character of others, he says, but run straight along the line, without swerving. A runner who keeps glancing sideways loses ground.
Some of the time we wish we had may already be in the day, leaking out sideways into other people's cars and kitchens and arguments. Close that leak, even partly, and the minutes come back.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius sometimes practice Meditations 4.18 by skipping one habit of checking on others, such as a feed, and spending the time on their own work.

o: a day off that the law gives every worker each week
the free time you get back by not watching your neighbors
the hours saved by doing two tasks at the same time

s: Marcus says stop caring about other people
he says stop monitoring them; caring is another thing.
Marcus uses a runner's image in this entry
run straight along the line, without swerving.
Marcus says the attention you take back goes to your own acts being just
look only at what you yourself are doing, he says, that it be just and holy.

games.q: you open an app and see that a friend just got the promotion you wanted. you feel the pull to scroll their whole page. what fits 4.18?
o: scroll it all, to see how they did it.
close it, and turn back to your own next task.
post something to look just as good.
games.why: Marcus says look only at what you yourself are doing, that it be just: the time you don't spend watching is time gained.

practice: Think of the place where you most often watch other people, a feed, a group chat, a neighbor's driveway, and picture reaching for it the way you usually do.
Then picture pausing, and turning your attention back to your own next task. Notice the minutes you just kept.

wordCard.voice: Time gained. Marcus says how much leisure you gain by not watching what your neighbor says, does or thinks, and only seeing that your own acts are just. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'good leisure, free time': what Marcus says you gain by not watching your neighbor.

carryVoice: Your line: run straight along the line, without swerving. Your own lane is work enough. Day five hundred fifty-five, done.
